title: Storage models and compression
lead: The same orders table can be easy to update one row at a time yet waste bytes in a report. Follow which fields are read before choosing a layout or an encoding.
goals: Compare row, column, and PAX layouts by the bytes read
Encode and decode RLE, delta, and dictionary representations
Distinguish a teaching model from the actual Parquet format

sections.title: Why a report reads fields it never uses
sections.html:
Suppose our shop stores Orders(id,city,amount). A cashier opens one order to change its city; the manager asks for total sales in city A. Both use the same table, but they need different portions of its bytes. Start with three original teaching rows: (1,A,10), (2,B,20), (3,A,30). The logical rows will stay the same throughout this lesson; only their physical arrangement changes.

Orders:
[1,A,10] [2,B,20] [3,A,30]

id:     [1,2,3]
city:   [A,B,A]
amount: [10,20,30]

In the row layout, reading order 2 brings its id, city and amount together. That helps the cashier. But a report testing city must pass the other fields in every row. In the column layout, test city first: A occurs at positions 1 and 3. Those positions identify the corresponding amount values, 10 and 30; add them to get 40. Finding positions is a separate step from gathering the requested values. To reconstruct order 2, gather position 2 from all three arrays: (2,B,20). Null information and variable-length values need metadata; these aligned arrays are a deliberately small model.

We can now name the workload distinction. OLTP, online transaction processing, typically touches a few complete records for short transactions. OLAP, online analytical processing, typically scans many records but a subset of their fields. HTAP combines both needs. These are workload tendencies, not rules that prohibit a query on another layout. Column storage improves locality when processing one field and often makes its values easier to compress; splitting and reconstructing complete rows adds work. The next question is how much unnecessary reading this can avoid.

sections.title: Count the bytes, then choose how much to group
sections.html:
Scale the shop to 1,000,000 records of 100 bytes each. The report uses city and amount, together 12 bytes per record. Assume a full scan, separately readable columns, no compression, headers or alignment padding, and decimal MB: 1 MB=1,000,000 bytes. The row layout reads 1,000,000×100=100 MB. The column layout reads 1,000,000×12=12 MB. Subtract: 100−12=88 MB avoided. Divide by the original size: 88/100=88%. The byte ratio is 100/12≈8.33; it describes input bytes, not a promised speedup. Gathering values, decoding and CPU work still take time.

Can we keep related rows in one bounded region while processing their fields together? Divide six rows into groups of three. Inside the first group store A=[a0,a1,a2], B=[b0,b1,b2], C=[c0,c1,c2]; inside the second store A=[a3,a4,a5], B=[b3,b4,b5], C=[c3,c4,c5]. This gives a hybrid arrangement. PAX, Partition Attributes Across, applies vertical grouping within a database page. A scan of one attribute can use cache lines more effectively, but if the disk API reads whole pages it still reads the whole containing PAX page.

Parquet uses a larger hierarchy: a file contains row groups; each group has one chunk per column; chunks contain encoded pages. A row group is not a buffer frame or a DBMS page. This hierarchy permits reading selected chunks and processing groups independently. It does not mean that our three-array drawing implements the Parquet format.

The report now needs every field of one order. Does the 88% saving still follow?

Reasoned answer. No. That calculation assumed a full scan using 12 of each record’s 100 bytes. A point lookup for a complete row has different access and reconstruction costs. State which fields and which rows are needed before reusing the calculation.

Key takeaway

A byte-count ratio of 8.33 does not guarantee an 8.33-fold speedup. The byte-count ratio in this example is approximately 8.33, but execution also includes reconstructing rows from separate columns, decompression, filtering, and other CPU work. The ratio describes the bytes read under the stated assumptions.

sections.title: Make repeated values and small differences cheaper
sections.html:
After avoiding unused fields, can we reduce the bytes of fields we still need? We require lossless encoding: decoding must reproduce every original value. The examples below are original exercises; they count payload, not every format header. A general-purpose codec compresses bytes without understanding cities or prices and usually needs a block decoded before examining its values. Column encodings can exploit the values themselves.

Start with [7,7,7,2,2,9]. Consecutive repetition lets us store [(7,3),(2,2),(9,1)], each pair meaning (value,count). Expanding the counts recovers the input. This is run-length encoding, RLE. SUM can work on the runs: 7×3+2×2+9×1=34. For [1,2,1,2], four one-value runs add count overhead rather than helping. Order affects compression even when the set of values is unchanged.

For [50,53,54,58,59], repeated values are absent but differences are small. Keep first=50. Subtract adjacent values: deltas=[3,1,4,1]. Keep minimum delta=1 and subtract it: residuals=[2,0,3,0]. The largest residual, 3, needs two unsigned bits. Decode in the reverse order: add 1 to get [3,1,4,1], then cumulatively add to 50: 50→53→54→58→59. A delta can be negative; its metadata must support that. Residuals are nonnegative because we subtracted the minimum, and at least one is zero. All-zero residuals can use zero payload bits while still needing the first value, minimum, count and format metadata. Real Parquet also has blocks, miniblocks and padding.

For [tea,cake,tea,juice], build one dictionary tea→0, cake→1, juice→2, then store [0,1,0,2]. Resolving tea once allows equality filtering on code 0. But code 0 is less than code 1 while tea sorts after cake: arbitrary dictionary codes do not preserve value order. Codes from different dictionaries may also mean different things. For 100 values drawn from four 10-byte ASCII strings, one-byte codes use 100 bytes and dictionary strings use 40: 140 payload bytes versus 1,000 raw bytes. With mostly distinct short values, dictionary overhead can reverse the saving.

Encode [8,10,11] using first value, minimum delta and residuals. Then decode it.

Reasoned answer. first=8; deltas=[2,1]; minimum=1; residuals=[1,0]. Add the minimum to recover [2,1]; 8+2=10 and 10+1=11. One bit per residual suffices, but it does not include metadata.

Key takeaway

Dictionary codes do not automatically preserve the original values’ order. Here tea has code 0 and cake has code 1, but cake comes before tea alphabetically. Comparing codes as ordered values is valid only when the code assignment preserves the required order.

sections.title: Use metadata to decide what can be skipped
sections.html:
A reader needs a map before it can fetch selected Parquet chunks. File metadata records schema and locations; the footer lets a reader find those locations. A writer can emit data in one pass, learn its offsets, and write metadata at the end. Row groups provide independent units for parallel work. Statistics may then eliminate regions before decoding their payload. Consider two chunks: C1 has minimum 10 and maximum 20; C2 has minimum 10 and maximum 50. For amount>30, C1 cannot match and may be skipped when these bounds are valid. C2 must be inspected. For amount=30, C2 is still only a candidate: its bounds do not prove that 30 actually occurs. Missing statistics do not justify skipping data.

The same care applies to bit packing. For 1,000 unsigned values in 0–7, each needs 3 bits: 1,000×3=3,000 bits, or 375 bytes. Storing each in 32 bits takes 4,000 bytes. If one value becomes 8 and the entire block shares one width, 3 bits no longer suffice; 4 bits per value gives 4,000 bits=500 bytes. These are payload sizes, not complete file sizes. A format can use other exception policies, but our chosen policy changes every value’s width.

A chunk has min=10,max=50 and no value 30. Can metadata alone answer amount=30? What if the predicate is amount>50?

Reasoned answer. The bounds cannot decide equality: read and test the surviving data to discover no match. They can exclude amount>50, provided the statistics are valid for the predicate. Distinguish “may match” from “does match”.

A real Parquet parser must additionally interpret schema, encodings, and repetition/definition levels for nested values. Slide size examples are configuration choices, not universal constants. Our arrays and byte counts explain the ideas; they are not a specification-conformant encoder. Compression trades fewer storage reads for encoding/decoding work; evaluate the whole query rather than treating the compression ratio as elapsed-time improvement.

quiz.question: What is the minimum number of bits per unsigned value needed to encode residual=[2,0,3,0]?
quiz.explanation: Two unsigned bits have four patterns, 00,01,10,11, representing 0 through 3. The residual maximum is 3, so two bits suffice; one bit would represent only 0 and 1. This counts residual payload, not the first value, minimum delta or format metadata.
